marrow__ANAT_CH36_Q001.takeaway: The axillary sheath around the axillary vessels and brachial plexus is an extension of prevertebral fascia.
marrow__ANAT_CH36_Q001.displayText: The fascia around the axillary vessels and brachial plexus is called the axillary sheath. It is derived from the prevertebral fascia. Clinical correlations in the source: in a brachial plexus nerve block the axillary sheath localizes anaesthetic solution to the plexus; a chronic retropharyngeal abscess in tuberculosis may spread to the axilla or superior mediastinum, but it never spreads to the posterior mediastinum because the supravertebral fascia fuses there to restrict spread.

It is derived from the prevertebral fascia

rationales.b: Clavipectoral fascia surrounds subclavius and pectoralis minor; it is not the source of the sheath around the plexus.
rationales.c: The investing layer encloses sternocleidomastoid and trapezius rather than forming the axillary sheath.
rationales.d: Superficial cervical fascia is not the deep fascial sleeve accompanying the axillary neurovascular bundle.

marrow__ANAT_CH36_Q002.takeaway: The thoracoacromial trunk pierces clavipectoral fascia, alongside the cephalic vein and lateral pectoral nerve.
marrow__ANAT_CH36_Q002.displayText: The labelled structure is the artery piercing the clavipectoral fascia, the thoracoacromial artery. Clavipectoral fascia envelops subclavius and pectoralis minor; medially it forms the costocoracoid ligament, and laterally it is connected to axillary fascia by the suspensory ligament of the axilla (Gerdy's ligament). Structures piercing clavipectoral fascia are one vein (cephalic vein), one artery (thoracoacromial artery with associated veins and lymphatics) and one nerve (lateral pectoral nerve).

rationales.a: The axillary artery is the parent vessel in the axilla; the structure piercing this fascia is its thoracoacromial branch.
rationales.c: The lateral thoracic artery descends along the thoracic wall and is not the artery identified piercing clavipectoral fascia.
rationales.d: The subscapular artery is a large third-part axillary branch; it does not match the source-described piercing vessel.

marrow__ANAT_CH36_Q003.takeaway: The triangular interval transmits the radial nerve and profunda brachii vessels; circumflex scapular vessels pass through the triangular space.
marrow__ANAT_CH36_Q003.displayText: The space around the shoulder joint where the radial nerve may be compressed is the triangular interval. It contains the profunda brachii vessels. Therefore, the statement that it contains the circumflex scapular vessels is false.
emphasis: The space around the shoulder joint where the radial nerve may be compressed is the triangular interval

rationales.a: Teres major forms the superior boundary of the triangular interval, so this is a true boundary rather than the false statement.
rationales.c: The humeral shaft forms the lateral boundary of the triangular interval.
rationales.d: The long head of triceps forms its medial boundary.

marrow__ANAT_CH36_Q004.takeaway: Quadrangular-space syndrome threatens the axillary nerve, which traverses the space with the posterior circumflex humeral vessels.
marrow__ANAT_CH36_Q004.displayText: The axillary nerve is likely to be affected because it is one of the contents of the quadrangular space. Quadrangular space syndrome is caused by hypertrophy or fibrosis of quadrangular-space muscles, impinging on the axillary nerve and producing weakness of shoulder movements.
emphasis: The axillary nerve is likely to be affected because it is one of the contents of the quadrangular space
Quadrangular space syndrome is caused by hypertrophy or fibrosis of quadrangular-space muscles, impinging on the axillary nerve and producing weakness of shoulder movements

rationales.a: The musculocutaneous nerve pierces coracobrachialis and travels in the anterior arm; it is not a quadrangular-space content.
rationales.b: The suprascapular nerve passes through the suprascapular notch and supplies supra-/infraspinatus, not through this space.
rationales.c: The radial nerve travels through the triangular interval with profunda brachii, rather than through quadrangular space.

marrow__ANAT_CH36_Q005.takeaway: The bicipital aponeurosis roofs the cubital fossa; the biceps tendon, brachial artery and median nerve lie within it.
marrow__ANAT_CH36_Q005.displayText: The bicipital aponeurosis is not a content of the cubital fossa; it forms the roof. The biceps tendon is a content of the cubital fossa. The source notes that the radial nerve is listed as a content in some books and excluded in others because of its extreme lateral position.

The source notes that the radial nerve is listed as a content in some books and excluded in others because of its extreme lateral position

rationales.a: The median nerve is a recognized cubital-fossa content, medial to the brachial artery.
rationales.c: The brachial artery and its bifurcation are within the fossa.
rationales.d: The radial nerve lies at the lateral side; some references omit it from the contents because of its very lateral position, a source-noted convention difference.

marrow__ANAT_CH36_Q006.takeaway: At the anatomical snuffbox, the superficial radial nerve and cephalic vein form the roof; the radial artery is the sole content.
marrow__ANAT_CH36_Q006.displayText: The marked region is the anatomical snuffbox. The superficial branch of the radial nerve forms the roof. Tenderness here suggests scaphoid fracture, a common injury after a fall on an outstretched hand. Boundaries: lateral wall - abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis; medial wall - extensor pollicis longus. Roof - cephalic vein and superficial branch of radial nerve. Floor - radial styloid, scaphoid, trapezium and first metacarpal. The only content is the radial artery.

The superficial branch of the radial nerve forms the roof

rationales.a: The radial artery lies in the floor/content of the snuffbox, not its roof.
rationales.b: The basilic vein is on the medial arm and does not cross the snuffbox roof.
rationales.d: The superficial ulnar nerve is not a roof structure of the radial-sided snuffbox.

marrow__ANAT_CH36_Q007.displayText: The lateral boundary of the anatomical snuffbox is formed by extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus. The medial wall is extensor pollicis longus; roof is cephalic vein plus superficial branch of the radial nerve; floor is radial styloid, scaphoid, trapezium and first metacarpal; only content is the radial artery.

marrow__ANAT_CH36_Q008.takeaway: The flexor carpi ulnaris tendon stays outside the carpal tunnel; the median nerve and FDS, FDP and FPL tendons pass within it.
marrow__ANAT_CH36_Q008.displayText: The clinical scenario is suggestive of carpal tunnel syndrome. The carpal tunnel does not contain flexor carpi ulnaris. Its contents comprise four flexor digitorum profundus tendons, four flexor digitorum superficialis tendons, one flexor pollicis longus tendon and the median nerve between the FDP and FDS tendons. Superficial to the carpal tunnel and flexor retinaculum, the ulnar artery and ulnar nerve pass through Guyon's canal.

rationales.a: Four FDP tendons are tunnel contents.
rationales.b: Four FDS tendons pass through the carpal tunnel.
rationales.c: The flexor pollicis longus tendon also traverses the tunnel.

marrow__ANAT_CH36_Q009.takeaway: Flexor carpi radialis occupies the lateral deep slip of the flexor retinaculum; the medial superficial slip roofs Guyon canal.
marrow__ANAT_CH36_Q009.displayText: Flexor carpi radialis is the only content in the lateral deep slip of the flexor retinaculum, not the medial slip. The flexor retinaculum has a medial superficial slip (volar carpal ligament) forming Guyon's canal, which contains the ulnar nerve and vessels; and a lateral deep slip containing only the FCR tendon. Attachments are medial to pisiform and hook of hamate, and lateral to the tubercles of scaphoid and trapezium.

Attachments are medial to pisiform and hook of hamate, and lateral to the tubercles of scaphoid and trapezium

rationales.a: The retinaculum attaches medially to pisiform and hook of hamate, so this attachment statement is true.
rationales.b: Its lateral attachments are the scaphoid and trapezium tubercles, making this statement true.
rationales.c: The source describes a medial superficial slip and a lateral deep slip; the error is assigning FCR to the medial slip.

marrow__ANAT_CH36_Q010.takeaway: The fourth extensor compartment contains extensor indicis, posterior interosseous nerve and anterior interosseous artery; EPL occupies the third compartment.
marrow__ANAT_CH36_Q010.displayText: Extensor pollicis longus is not present in the fourth compartment of the extensor retinaculum. The fourth compartment contains extensor indicis, posterior interosseous nerve and anterior interosseous artery. The extensor retinaculum attaches medially to pisiform and triquetral, and laterally to the anterior border of radius.

marrow__ANAT_CH36_Q011.takeaway: Lumbricals and interossei insert into the extensor expansion as wing tendons; extensor digitorum forms the expansion rather than the wing tendons.
marrow__ANAT_CH36_Q011.displayText: Wing tendons refer to the insertion of lumbricals and interossei to the corners of the dorsal digital (extensor) expansion or simply extensor expansion, not to the attachment of extensor digitorum. The expansion is formed by extensor tendons expanding on the back of digits; the apex is at the distal phalanx, central region attaches to the middle phalanx (in the thumb to proximal phalanx), and the base is at the sides of the MCP joint. The central and collateral slips distribute the extensor mechanism to middle and distal phalanges.

rationales.c: The central slip inserts on the base of the middle phalanx (in the thumb, the proximal phalanx).
rationales.d: The collateral slips reach the distal phalanx, as stated in the source.

marrow__ANAT_CH36_Q012.takeaway: Kanavel signs point to flexor-sheath tenosynovitis: tendon tenderness, fusiform swelling, semiflexed posture and pain on passive extension.
marrow__ANAT_CH36_Q012.displayText: Kanavel's sign is suggestive of tenosynovitis. It helps distinguish infectious tenosynovitis from superficial or localized abscess. Kanavel's signs are tenderness over the affected tendon, fusiform swelling over the affected tendon, the affected finger held in slight flexion, and pain on passive extension.

It helps distinguish infectious tenosynovitis from superficial or localized abscess
Kanavel's signs are tenderness over the affected tendon, fusiform swelling over the affected tendon, the affected finger held in slight flexion, and pain on passive extension

rationales.b: Dupuytren contracture is palmar fascial fibrosis with fixed finger flexion, not the acute tendon-sheath signs described.
rationales.c: Carpal tunnel syndrome causes median-nerve compression symptoms at the wrist rather than Kanavel signs in an infected digit.
rationales.d: Trigger finger is catching from stenosing tenosynovitis at a pulley, not the full Kanavel pattern of infectious flexor-sheath involvement.

marrow__ANAT_CH36_Q013.takeaway: Middle- and ring-finger infections can enter the mid-palmar space; index-finger infections more often track to thenar space.
marrow__ANAT_CH36_Q013.displayText: The image shows paronychia of the middle finger. Infection of the ring and middle fingers spreads into the mid-palmar space; index-finger infection spreads to the thenar space; little-finger infection spreads to the ulnar bursa and mid-palmar space.

rationales.b: Ulnar bursa is associated with the little-finger flexor sheath.
rationales.d: Thenar space is the source-listed destination for index-finger infection, not this middle-finger case.

marrow__ANAT_CH36_Q014.takeaway: The first lumbrical accompanies the index-finger FDP tendon in the thenar space; lumbricals 2–4 relate to mid-palmar tendons.
marrow__ANAT_CH36_Q014.displayText: The first lumbrical is not a content of the mid-palmar space. It is related to the FDP tendon of the index finger (second digit) and lies in the thenar space. The second, third and fourth lumbricals are related to the FDP tendons of the middle, ring and little fingers, respectively, and lie in the mid-palmar space.

rationales.b: The third FDP tendon is among the mid-palmar contents.
rationales.c: The second lumbrical accompanies the middle-finger FDP tendon and is in the mid-palmar space.
